title: Revenue, COGS, and Gross Profit
subtitle: The first three lines of the P&L - the foundation of every analysis
openingQuestion: A company sells 1,000 units at 100k each, with a cost of 60k per unit. What is Gross Profit?
explanation: The first three lines of the income statement tell a tight little story: how much did we sell (Revenue), how much did it cost to make exactly that amount of goods (COGS), and what's left over (Gross Profit). COGS only covers direct costs - raw materials, production labour - not office salaries or marketing; those sit further down. That boundary matters, because it decides whether the gross margin reflects production efficiency rather than operating efficiency.

diagram.label: Subtract the direct cost of making exactly that amount of goods
Divide by revenue to get gross margin - a measure of pricing power

realWorldExample.description: Vinamilk is a textbook example of a stable Gross Margin in the FMCG sector. Revenue comes mainly from liquid milk, milk powder, and yoghurt; COGS covers raw milk costs (imported milk powder, purchased fresh milk), packaging, and direct production labour. Thanks to scale and a strong brand, Vinamilk's Gross Margin has typically held around 40%, well above many smaller rivals in the industry - evidence of pricing power and supply-chain efficiency.

quiz.question: What is Revenue?
options: The profit left over after subtracting every cost
The cost of producing the goods that were sold
The actual cash collected during the period
The total value of sales, before subtracting any cost
quiz.explanation: Revenue is recognised at delivery (accrual), regardless of when the cash is actually received.

quiz.question: What is COGS?
options: The direct cost of producing the goods that were sold
Every cost the business incurs during the period
Interest expense the business must pay
Selling, marketing, and administrative expenses
quiz.explanation: COGS = Cost of Goods Sold. It only covers production costs, not office salaries, marketing, etc.

quiz.question: Gross Profit = ?
options: Revenue + COGS
Revenue - COGS
Revenue × COGS
Revenue - OpEx
quiz.explanation: Gross Profit = Revenue - COGS, profit before OpEx. It reflects production/sales efficiency.

quiz.question: Is a high Gross Margin (GM), say 60%, always good?
options: No, the lower it is, the better
Yes - it means production/sales are efficient and production costs are low
It depends on the industry: 20-30% is already good for retail, software needs 70-80%
Yes, and it can be compared directly across any industry
quiz.explanation: A high GM means the product carries a good margin. But it depends on the industry: a 20-30% GM is normal for Retail, while 70-80% is normal for Software.

quiz.question: Between a retail store and a software company, which one has the higher Gross Margin?
options: Retail is higher because it sells much larger volumes
They can't be compared, since the two industries are completely different
They're equal, since both use the same formula
Software is higher because the cost of an extra copy is close to zero
quiz.explanation: Retail: buy for 10, sell for 15, GM = 33%. Software: sell for a million, production cost near zero, GM = 90%+.

quiz.question: Company A: Revenue 1000, COGS 400. Gross Profit = ?
options: 1400 (added instead of subtracted)
400 (mistakenly used COGS itself as the answer)
250 (= 1000 / 400, divided instead of subtracted)

quiz.question: If Revenue rises but Gross Profit falls, what does that signal?
options: The business is selling more goods than before
COGS is growing faster than Revenue
Interest expense has increased
Selling and administrative expenses are growing faster than revenue
quiz.explanation: Selling more but seeing gross profit fall means production costs are rising - a warning sign.

quiz.question: What does COGS include?
options: The business's entire operating cost for the period
Office salaries, marketing, and administrative expenses
Production wages, raw materials, and factory energy costs
Interest expense and corporate income tax owed
quiz.explanation: COGS = direct costs. Marketing, admin, and R&D are Operating Expense, not COGS.

quiz.question: If a company wants to improve Gross Profit, what should it do?
options: Cut the selling price to move more volume during the period
Cut marketing and administrative spending
Borrow more capital to expand production capacity faster
Raise prices, cut COGS, or shift the product mix
quiz.explanation: GP = Revenue - COGS. Raising Revenue or cutting COGS both improve GP.

quiz.question: A company sells two products: A (GP 30%) and B (GP 50%). To optimise profit, what should it do?
options: Sell more of B, since it carries the higher margin
Sell only A, to keep its largest customer base
Sell only B, and drop A entirely
Keep the mix at 50-50 to spread out risk
quiz.explanation: Mix management: selling more of the higher-margin product raises gross profit, as long as the cost of selling it doesn't rise too much.

quiz.question: A company raises its selling price by 10% while keeping COGS per unit unchanged. What happens to Gross Margin (as a %)?
options: It stays the same, since COGS per unit is unchanged
Gross Margin rises
Gross Margin falls
It can't be determined without knowing SG&A costs
quiz.explanation: Gross Margin % = Gross Profit / Revenue. If price rises while unit production cost stays flat, gross profit per unit rises by exactly the price increase - lifting Gross Margin % accordingly. This is why pricing power (raising price without losing customers) is so valuable.

keyTakeaways: COGS = the direct cost of making the product
Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue - a measure of pricing power

practicePrompt.question: A garment workshop sells shirts at 300k each. Fabric, thread, and direct sewing labour cost 180k per shirt; allocated office rent and accounting salaries add another 40k per shirt. Which of these two cost items counts as COGS?
options: Only the 40k of office rent and accounting salaries counts as COGS, because it's a fixed monthly cost
The 180k (fabric, thread, direct sewing labour) is COGS - because it's the direct cost of making the product; the 40k belongs to SG&A (indirect operating cost)
The full 220k counts as COGS, because all of it is spending the company must make to sell the product
Neither amount counts as COGS, because COGS only applies to large-scale manufacturers
practicePrompt.explanation: COGS = the direct cost of making the product (fabric, thread, sewing labour). Indirect management costs (office rent, accounting salaries) belong to SG&A, below Gross Profit. Gross Profit = 300k - 180k = 120k per shirt; Gross Margin = 120/300 = 40%.

summary.keyIdea: COGS = the direct cost of making the product
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate a company's own Gross Margin
application.message: The lesson already gave a real example with FPT's Gross Margin (39.2%) - see the 'Real example' section above. Now calculate the Gross Margin of another company yourself from its latest financial statements.
application.secondary: Comparing that margin against a peer in the same industry is more interesting than looking at it alone.

sections.text: The first three lines of the Income Statement - Revenue, COGS, Gross Profit - are the foundation for every deeper analysis. Misread these three lines and every ratio calculated afterward drifts along with them.
Revenue: more than just 'how much money came in'

Revenue is the total value of goods/services delivered to customers during the period, recognised under the accrual principle rather than when cash lands in the account. A company can report large revenue while the actual cash comes in much later - which is why you need to cross-check against the Cash Flow Statement.
COGS: the direct cost tied to the product

Cost of Goods Sold is the full direct cost of producing the goods or services that were sold: raw materials, direct production labour, allocated factory overhead. The key point: COGS is only counted for the portion of goods actually SOLD, not everything produced - unsold inventory still sits on the Balance Sheet as Inventory.

Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS. This is the profit left after subtracting direct cost, before subtracting any other operating expense. Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue, measuring the percentage of revenue kept after cost of goods - an important indicator of pricing power and competitive advantage.

items: Revenue: recognised on an accrual basis, not as actual cash collected.
COGS: direct cost, counted only for goods/services actually sold.
A high Gross Margin usually comes with a strong brand or a cost advantage.

left.label: High Gross Margin (40-70%)
left.text: Common among companies with strong brands or differentiated products - for example branded consumer goods, software, and pharmaceuticals.

right.label: Low Gross Margin (5-20%)
right.text: Common in industries competing on price, or that are capital-intensive or distribution-heavy - for example retail, trading, and logistics.

concepts.def: The total value of goods/services delivered during the period, recognised on an accrual basis
The direct cost of producing the goods that were sold
Gross Profit divided by Revenue, expressed as a %

sections.text: A real example: FPT's Gross Margin

items: Gross Margin: 39.2% (Q1/2025) versus 37.7% for full-year 2024 - meaning for every 100 dong of revenue, FPT keeps about 39.2 dong after subtracting cost of goods sold (COGS), before subtracting selling/admin costs further down

A gross margin improving over time is usually a good sign: the company is selling more efficiently or shifting toward higher-margin segments (for example FPT shifting toward IT/AI services, which carry a higher margin than hardware)

sections.label: How to calculate it yourself, without ready-made numbers
sections.text: Open the income statement, take net revenue minus cost of goods sold to get Gross Profit, then divide Gross Profit by net revenue to get Gross Margin - work it out yourself to be sure you understand the formula correctly, rather than relying on a number a brokerage has already computed for you.

lines: Gross Margin is the first metric to check when comparing the competitive strength of companies in the same industry.
